newsitem.title: USA: U.S. energy secretary choice faces Senate grilling.
newsitem.headline: U.S. energy secretary choice faces Senate grilling.

text.p: President Clinton's choice for energy secretary, Federico Pena, faces tough questions at his confirmation hearing on how he plans to dispose of nuclear waste and on why the Energy Department should not be abolished, Senate sources said Wednesday.

The Senate Energy Committee is to hold a hearing Thursday on Pena's bid to switch Cabinet positions from transportation secretary to energy. While most sources said they expected the nomination to be approved and sent to the full Senate, they said some senators had concerns about the administration's energy policies and about Pena's qualifications.

"I would assume right now that he would be voted out of committee and sent to the floor. There might be some reservations by some senators or questions that we want to ask about DOE (the Department of Energy)," Sen. Rod Grams, a Minnesota Republican, said at a news conference on a bill to eliminate the department.

Grams said his bill was aimed at closing a department that he said had little purpose, not at Pena as incoming secretary. He said someone would have to direct the transition while Energy Department functions were farmed out to other agencies, adding that he would not necessarily vote against Pena.

Committee chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, has said he would press Pena on how the administration plans to dispose of spent nuclear reactor fuel and other nuclear waste accumulating at sites across the country.

Murkowski has pushed a bill to force the administration to set up a temporary dump site for waste from utilities' reactors and other sources. But Clinton threatened to veto the bill last session, saying it was environmentally unsound and would detract from efforts to establish a permanent dump.
States and utilities have sued the Energy Department to take over the waste by January 1998, as is called for in a nuclear policy law.

"Mr. Pena was a mayor and when he was mayor he was interested in moving waste from Rocky Flats out of the state," a spokesman for Murkowski said, referring to Pena's time as Denver's mayor and his efforts to get waste removed from the nearby Rocky Flats nuclear weapons facility.

Murkowski also "is concerned about the lack of a national strategy to wean us from oil imports," slow progress in cleaning up former nuclear weapons sites such as Rocky Flats, and the administration's stance on electric utility restructuring, his spokesman said.

Sen. Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said last month he thought Pena would "run into some trouble" being confirmed because he had little background in Energy Department issues. But Domenici's spokesman said he had met with Pena and "he's leaning toward supporting the nomination."
Domenici, who has major Energy Department laboratories and facilities in his state, wanted assurances that the facilities would be retained, his spokesman said.

Senate Republican Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma, who also serves on the committee, has not said how he was leaning on Pena's nomination, his spokesman said. But Nickles is a frequent critic of the administration's energy policies.
